events.title: Treaty of London guarantees Belgian neutrality
events.summary: Treaties signed in London on 19 April 1839 recognised Belgium as an independent and perpetually neutral state, with Britain among the signatory powers.
events.description: Treaties signed in London on 19 April 1839 by Britain, Austria, France, Prussia, Russia and the Netherlands settled the separation of Belgium from the Netherlands. Article VII stated that Belgium would form an independent and perpetually neutral state. In August 1914 the Belgian government cited the treaties of 1839 when it rejected Germany's request for passage, and the Imperial War Museums states that Germany's violation of Belgian neutrality and British fears of German domination in Europe brought Britain into the war on 4 August.

citations.quote: TREATIES RELATIVE TO THE NETHERLANDS AND BELGIUM signed at London, April 19, 1839.

Her Majesty the Queen of the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland, His Majesty the Emperor of Austria, King of Hungary and Bohemia, His Majesty the King of the French, His Majesty the King of Prussia, and His Majesty the Emperor of all the Russias, having taken into consideration their Treaty concluded with His Majesty the King of the Belgians, on the 15th of November 1831; and His Majesty the King of the Netherlands, Grand Duke of Luxembourg, being disposed to conclude a definite arrangement on the basis of the 24 Articles agreed upon by the Plenipotentiaries of Great Britain, Austria, France, Prussia, and Russia on the 14th of October, 1831; their said Majesties have named for their Plenipotentiaries, that is to say: * * * Who, after having communicated to each other their Full Powers, found in good and due form, have agreed upon the following Articles: ARTICLE I His Majesty the King of the Netherlands, Grand Duke of Luxembourg, engages to cause to be immediately converted into a Treaty with His Majesty the King of the Belgians, the Articles annexed to the present Act, and agreed upon by common consent, under the auspices of the Courts of Great Britain, Austria, France, Prussia and Russia. ARTICLE II Her Majesty the Queen of the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland, His Majesty the Emperor of Austria, King of Hungary and Bohemia, His Majesty the King of the French, His Majesty the King of Prussia, and His Majesty the Emperor of all the Russias declare

The union which has existed between Holland and Belgium, in virtue of the Treaty of Vienna, of the 31st of May, 1815, is acknowledged by His Majesty the King of the Netherlands, Grand Duke of Luxembourg, to be dissolved.
Belgium within the limits specified in Articles I, II and IV shall form an independent and perpetually neutral State.
This would be in direct violation of Belgium’s neutrality, which had been guaranteed in a treaty signed by major European powers, including Britain, in 1839.
The treaties of 1839, confirmed by the treaties of 1870 vouch for the independence and neutrality of Belgium under the guarantee of the Powers
The Belgian Government, if they were to accept the proposals submitted to them, would sacrifice the honour of the nation and betray their duty towards Europe.
Germany's violation of Belgian neutrality and British fears of German domination in Europe brought Britain and its empire into the war on 4 August.

events.title: Congress of Berlin revises the Russo-Turkish peace
events.summary: The Congress of Berlin replaced the Treaty of San Stefano, reduced Russia's gains under it and allowed Austria-Hungary to occupy Bosnia and Herzegovina.
events.description: The major European powers met in Berlin from 13 June to 13 July 1878 and replaced the Treaty of San Stefano, signed by Russia and Turkey after the Russo-Turkish War of 1877–78. Britannica writes that the revised settlement satisfied British interests by denying Russia the means to extend its naval power, allowed Austria-Hungary to occupy Bosnia and Herzegovina, and left Russia humiliated by substantially reducing the gains it had made at San Stefano, and that the congress failed to consider adequately the aspirations of the Balkan peoples. Foster writes that over the following decades Austria-Hungary's presence in Bosnia brought it into conflict with regional actors, of whom Serbian nationalists were the most antagonistic.

citations.quote: Congress of Berlin, (June 13–July 13, 1878), diplomatic meeting of the major European powers at which the Treaty of Berlin replaced the Treaty of San Stefano, which had been signed by Russia and Turkey (March 3, 1878) at the conclusion of the Russo-Turkish War of 1877–78.
to satisfy the interests of Great Britain (by denying Russia the means to extend its naval power and by maintaining the Ottoman Empire as a European power)
to satisfy the interests of Austria-Hungary (by allowing it to occupy Bosnia and Herzegovina and thereby increase its influence in the Balkans)
the congress left Russia humiliated by substantially reducing the gains that it had made under the San Stefano treaty
the congress failed to consider adequately the aspirations of the Balkan peoples themselves
Article 25 of the Treaty of Berlin (July 13,1878) gave Austria-Hungary the right to occupy and administer the two provinces of Bosnia and Herzegovina.
Over the following decades, the Dual Monarchy’s presence in the territory, still nominally under the rule of the Ottoman Sultan, brought it into conflict with various regional actors.
Among these, Serbian nationalists proved the most antagonistic, perceiving Bosnia-Herzegovina’s large Serb minority as an integral part of a historic “Greater Serbia”.

events.title: Dual Alliance between Germany and Austria-Hungary
events.summary: Germany and Austria-Hungary signed a secret defensive treaty on 7 October 1879, promising each other full military support if either was attacked by Russia.
events.description: On 7 October 1879 Germany and Austria-Hungary signed a secret treaty. Each promised to help the other with its full military strength if Russia attacked either of them. If another power attacked one of them, the other would remain at least benevolently neutral, and the full mutual-assistance obligation would apply if Russia supported that attacker by active cooperation or by military measures that threatened the party attacked. The Imperial War Museums states that Germany allied with Austria-Hungary in 1879 and that Italy joined three years later.

citations.quote: 7 October, 1879 The Dual Alliance Between Austria-Hungary and Germany
one of the two Empires be attacked by Russia the High Contracting Parties are bound to come to the assistance one of the other with the whole war strength of their Empires

Should one of the High Contracting Parties be attacked by another Power, the other High Contracting Party binds itself hereby, not only not to support the aggressor against its high Ally, but to observe at least a benevolent neutral attitude towards its fellow Contracting Party.

Should, however, the attacking party in such a case be supported by Russia, either by an active cooperation or by military measures which constitute a menace to the Party attacked, then the obligation stipulated in Article 1 of this Treaty, for reciprocal assistance with the whole fighting force, becomes equally operative
be kept secret by the two High Contracting Parties
This new power bloc at the heart of central Europe strengthened further when Germany formed an alliance in 1879 with neighbouring Austria-Hungary, which Italy joined three years later.

events.title: Italy joins Germany and Austria-Hungary in the Triple Alliance
events.summary: On 20 May 1882 Italy, Germany and Austria-Hungary signed a secret treaty of mutual help against unprovoked French attacks on Italy or Germany and, under further conditions, other great powers.
events.description: The Triple Alliance treaty, signed in Vienna on 20 May 1882, bound Germany and Austria-Hungary to help Italy if France attacked it without direct provocation, and Italy to help Germany in the same case. If one or two of the parties, without direct provocation on their part, were attacked by and engaged in war with two or more great powers that had not signed the treaty, the obligation applied to all three. The treaty was to be kept secret.

citations.quote: In case Italy, without direct provocation on her part, should be attacked by France for any reason whatsoever, the two other Contracting Parties shall be bound to lend help and assistance with all their forces to the Party attacked.
This same obligation shall devolve upon Italy in case of any aggression without direct provocation by France against Germany.

If one, or two, of the High Contracting Parties, without direct provocation on their part, should chance to be attacked and to be engaged in a war with two or more Great Powers non-signatory to the present Treaty, the casus foederis will arise simultaneously for all the High Contracting Parties.
The High Contracting Parties mutually promise secrecy as to the contents and existence of the present Treaty.
Done at Vienna, the twentieth day of the month of May of the year one thousand eight hundred and eighty-two.
Germany formed an alliance in 1879 with neighbouring Austria-Hungary, which Italy joined three years later.

events.title: France and Russia form a military alliance
events.summary: A secret military convention signed in 1892 and in force by 1894 committed France and Russia to mobilise together if the Triple Alliance or any of its members mobilised.
events.description: France and Russia signed a secret military convention on 18 August 1892, stating that its purpose was a defensive war against an attack by the forces of the Triple Alliance. If Germany, or Italy or Austria supported by Germany, attacked either country, the other would employ all its available forces to attack Germany, so that Germany would have to fight in the east and the west at once. If the Triple Alliance or any one of its members mobilised, both countries would mobilise at once, and all the clauses were to be kept absolutely secret. The Imperial War Museums attributes the alliance to fear of Germany's growing strength.

citations.quote: 18 August, 1892 The Franco-Russian Alliance Military Convention
having no other object than to meet the necessities of a defensive war, provoked by an attack of the forces of the Triple Alliance against either of them

If France is attacked by Germany, or by Italy supported by Germany, Russia shall employ all her available forces to attack Germany. If Russia is attacked by Germany, or by Austria supported by Germany, France shall employ all her available forces to attack Germany.

In case the forces of the Triple Alliance, or of any one of the Powers belonging to it, should be mobilized, France and Russia, at the first news of this event and without previous agreement being necessary, shall mobilize immediately and simultaneously the whole of their forces
These forces shall engage to the full with such speed that Germany will have to fight simultaneously on the East and on the West.
All the clauses enumerated above shall be kept absolutely secret.
Fear of Germany’s growing strength encouraged Russia and France to enter into alliance in 1893.

events.title: Entente Cordiale between Britain and France
events.summary: The Anglo-French agreement of 8 April 1904 settled colonial disputes, giving Britain a free hand in Egypt and France a free hand in Morocco.
events.description: The agreement of 8 April 1904 settled a number of disputes between Britain and France, most importantly by granting Britain freedom of action in Egypt and France in Morocco. It was not an alliance and did not tie Britain to France's 1894 commitment to Russia. Britannica writes that it opened the way to Anglo-French diplomatic cooperation against German pressure in the following decade.

citations.quote: Entente Cordiale, (April 8, 1904), Anglo-French agreement that, by settling a number of controversial matters, ended antagonisms between Great Britain and France and paved the way for their diplomatic cooperation against German pressures in the decade preceding World War I (1914–18).
The most important feature of the agreement was that it granted freedom of action to Great Britain in Egypt and to France in Morocco
The agreement in no sense created an alliance and did not entangle Great Britain with a French commitment to Russia (1894).
Britain had long seen France and Russia as potential enemies, but from 1904 it negotiated agreements with them, aiming to secure its empire by settling colonial disputes.

events.title: First Moroccan Crisis begins with the Kaiser's visit to Tangier
events.summary: On 31 March 1905 Wilhelm II landed at Tangier and declared for Moroccan independence, opposing French control; the Algeciras Conference settled the crisis in 1906.
events.description: On 31 March 1905 Emperor Wilhelm II visited Tangier and declared for the independence and integrity of Morocco, where France was seeking control. A German envoy's report records that the Kaiser told the French agent he wanted free trade and equal rights for Germany. The crisis ended at the Algeciras Conference in 1906, which entrusted policing in Morocco to France and Spain.

citations.quote: the emperor William II visited Tangier and, from his yacht on March 31, 1905, declared for Morocco’s independence and integrity.
After overcoming the difficult technical task of landing in Tangier, there was a very fitting reception on the dock by Moroccan officials and the German colony.
Moroccan crises, (1905–06, 1911), two international crises centring on France’s attempts to control Morocco and on Germany’s concurrent attempts to stem French power.
the Kaiser replied that his visit meant that His Majesty wanted free trade for Germany and complete equality of rights with other countries.

was resolved in January–April 1906 at the Algeciras Conference, where German and other national economic rights were upheld and where the French and Spanish were entrusted with the policing of Morocco.

events.title: Schlieffen submits his war plan
events.summary: In 1905 Alfred von Schlieffen, chief of the German general staff, submitted a war plan that sent German forces through neutral Belgium against France; a modified version was used in 1914.
events.description: Britannica describes the plan Alfred von Schlieffen proposed in 1905 as designed to let Germany win a two-front war, with France defeated first by forces passing through neutral Belgium while Russia was held off. A 1929 review in The Army Quarterly reports that the plan was worked out for war on the Western front only, because Russia was still weak after the Manchurian War, and that it provided for sending ten divisions east if Russia intervened. His successor Helmuth von Moltke modified the plan before and during its use in 1914, and Britannica notes that summaries of Schlieffen's studies found after 1956 opened new debates about his intentions and about how the plan was implemented.

citations.quote: battle plan first proposed in 1905 by Alfred, Graf (count) von Schlieffen, chief of the German general staff, that was designed to allow Germany to wage a successful two-front war
He decided that France was the enemy to be defeated first, with Russia held off until the French were annihilated.
Those forces were to wheel south and east after passing through neutral Belgium, turning into the flanks and rear of the hardened French defenses along the German border.
The plan was heavily modified by Schlieffen’s successor, Helmuth von Moltke, prior to and during its implementation in World War I.

Gerhard Ritter, a prominent German historian, published those studies in 1956 and concluded that the Schlieffen Plan was German doctrine prior to World War I. Further summaries have been discovered over subsequent decades, opening new debates about Schlieffen’s true intentions and the implementation of his plan.
It emerges incidentally that the Schlieffen plan was worked out for war on the Western front only; for when drawn up, Russia was still very weak as a result of the Manchurian War.
There was only a general statement that in the case of Russia intervening, ten divisions should be withdrawn from the Western front and sent to the East
submitted his plan in 1905; it was adopted, slightly modified, in 1914.

events.title: Anglo-Russian Convention settles disputes in Asia
events.summary: In 1907 Britain and Russia settled their disputes over Persia, Afghanistan and Tibet, an agreement that led to the Triple Entente with France.
events.description: In 1907 Britain and Russia divided Persia into spheres of influence, agreed not to interfere in Tibet's internal affairs and recognised British influence over Afghanistan. Britannica writes that the agreement led to the formation of the Triple Entente. The Imperial War Museums writes that the new friendship among the three powers increased German fears of encirclement.

citations.quote: pact in which Britain and Russia settled their colonial disputes in Persia, Afghanistan, and Tibet.
It delineated spheres of influence in Persia, stipulated that neither country would interfere in Tibet’s internal affairs, and recognized Britain’s influence over Afghanistan.
The agreement led to the formation of the Triple Entente.
The new and unlikely friendship between these three powers heightened German fears of ‘encirclement’ and deepened the divide among the European powers.

events.title: Austria-Hungary annexes Bosnia and Herzegovina
events.summary: Austria-Hungary announced the annexation of Bosnia and Herzegovina, which it had occupied since 1878, on 6 October 1908; Russia and Serbia recognised it by 1909.
events.description: Article 25 of the Treaty of Berlin had given Austria-Hungary the right to occupy and administer Bosnia and Herzegovina, and on 6 October 1908 it announced their formal annexation. Foster writes that the Young Turk Revolution of July 1908 served as the catalyst and that Vienna acted while Russia was militarily weakened by the war with Japan. He also writes that Vienna had obtained Russian approval for a future annexation in 1881, and that St Petersburg reneged on that agreement after Nicholas II's accession in 1894. After an initial diplomatic backlash, Russia and Serbia formally recognised the transfer of sovereignty by 1909.

citations.quote: Article 25 of the Treaty of Berlin (July 13,1878) gave Austria-Hungary the right to occupy and administer the two provinces of Bosnia and Herzegovina.
Austria-Hungary in 1908 annexed Bosnia and Herzegovina, which was announced formally on October 6, 1908.
The Young Turk Revolution in July 1908 subsequently served as the catalyst for direct action by the Monarchy.

Vienna took advantage of the political chaos within the Ottoman Empire and Russia’s diminished military capabilities, following the 1905 Russo-Japanese War, and announced that it would be formally annexing Bosnia-Herzegovina.
In 1881, Vienna had sought, and initially obtained, Germany and Russia’s approval for the future political annexation of its new Balkan protectorate.
The 1894 accession of Nicholas II, Emperor of Russia (1868-1918), however, saw St. Petersburg renege on its earlier agreements
by 1909, even Russia and Serbia had formally recognized Bosnia-Herzegovina’s transfer of sovereignty.

perspectives.wanted: Franz Joseph told Wilhelm II that the provinces had for some time wanted a constitution and that the changes in the Ottoman Empire had made this wish so strong that his government could no longer oppose it; Foster adds that Vienna sought to reassert political dominance over Serbia.
perspectives.feared: Foster writes that Vienna wanted to prevent the Young Turk Revolution from spreading northwards into the provinces.

citations.quote: While these provinces, which have progressed culturally and materially in so gratifying a manner, have expressed a desire for some time to establish a constitution, these aims now, because of the altered state of affairs in the Ottoman Empire, have asserted themselves so vigorously that my Government no longer feels that it can oppose them
citations.locator: Francis Joseph to Wilhelm II, September 29, 1908

citations.quote: seeking to prevent the revolution from spreading northwards while reasserting political dominance over Serbia

perspectives.wanted: Serbian leaders hoped for an eventual union of the people of Bosnia and Herzegovina with Serbia, which the annexation ruled out.
perspectives.feared: The Serbian government was deeply resentful of the annexation but judged that it could not challenge one of the great powers.

citations.quote: Deeply resentful of Austria-Hungary’s action, which excluded an eventual union of the inhabitants of Bosnia and Herzegovina with Serbia, the Serbian government nevertheless realized that it could not challenge one of the great powers.

perspectives.wanted: The society's 1911 programme called for preparation for war in all forms of national work, so that a new blow like the annexation would be met by a Serbia in which every Serb was a rifleman.
perspectives.feared: It described the annexation as one of many blows aimed at Serbia by its enemies and wrote that new enemies from the North wanted to take Serbia's freedom and language.

citations.quote: The annexation [ of Bosnia and Herzegovina ] was only one of the blows which the enemies of Serbia have aimed at this land.
The object assigned to the work to be done by the people of every class is the preparation for war in all forms of national work, corresponding to the requirements of the present day.
A new blow, like that of the annexation, must be met by a new Serbia, in which every Serbian, from child to greybeard, is a rifleman.
They want to take our freedom and our language from us and to crush us.

events.title: Žerajić's attempt on Governor Varešanin; Young Bosnia turns militant
events.summary: In June 1910 the Bosnian Serb Bogdan Žerajić tried to assassinate the governor of Bosnia, General Marijan Varešanin; groups such as Young Bosnia became more militant.
events.description: In June 1910 the Bosnian Serb Bogdan Žerajić attempted to assassinate General Marijan Varešanin, the Austro-Hungarian governor of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Foster writes that the attempt inspired organisations such as Young Bosnia (Mlada Bosna) to become increasingly militant. General Oskar Potiorek, appointed as Varešanin's successor in 1911, tried to suppress anti-Habsburg activity.

citations.quote: Inspired by the Bosnian Serb Bogdan Žerajić’s (1886-1910) attempted assassination of the provincial governor General Marijan Varešanin (1847-1917) in June 1910, so- called “cultural organisations”, such as “Young Bosnia” (Mlada Bosna), became increasingly militant.
This was compounded by the appointment of the politically ambitious General Oskar Potiorek (1853- 1933) as Varešanin’s successor in 1911.

The new governor’s efforts to suppress anti-Habsburg activities, following Serbia’s success during the Balkan Wars, brought Young Bosnia under the influence of the Serbian nationalist Black Hand Society.

events.title: Union or Death (the Black Hand) is founded in Serbia
events.summary: The secret society Union or Death, known as the Black Hand, was founded in Serbia in May 1911 to pursue the unification of all Serbs by revolutionary means.
events.description: Union or Death, better known as the Black Hand, was founded in Serbia in May 1911. Its constitution set the unification of all Serbs as its aim, gave priority to revolutionary struggle over cultural work and made the organisation secret. Britannica writes that it infiltrated the patriotic society Narodna Odbrana, which was active within the Serbian administration.

citations.quote: the patriotic society Narodna Odbrana (“National Defense”), invigorated by the infiltration of the “Union or Death” group (founded in May 1911 and better known as the Black Hand), was active not only within the Serbian administration
For the purpose of realising the national ideals - the Unification of Serbdom - an organization is hereby created
The organisation gives priority to the revolutionary struggle rather than relies on cultural striving, therefore its institution is an absolutely secret one for wider circles.

perspectives.wanted: The society sought Serbian unification, influence over official institutions in Serbia and revolutionary organisation wherever Serbs lived, and its constitution pledged it to fight with all means beyond Serbia's frontiers against all enemies of that idea.

citations.quote: For the purpose of realising the national ideals - the Unification of Serbdom - an organization is hereby created
it will exercise its influence over all the official factors in Serbia - which is the Piemont of Serbdom - as also over all the strata of the State and over the entire social life in it
It will carry out a revolutionary organisation in all the territories where Serbians are living
Beyond the frontiers, it will fight with all means against all enemies of this idea

perspectives.wanted: After 1908 the Serbian government judged that it could not challenge Austria-Hungary directly and turned its attention to Macedonia.

citations.quote: the Serbian government nevertheless realized that it could not challenge one of the great powers. It therefore turned its attention to Macedonia

events.title: Agadir Crisis over Morocco
events.summary: In 1911 Germany sent the gunboat Panther to Agadir to protest French influence in Morocco; Britain warned Germany and backed France.
events.description: In 1911 Germany sent the gunboat Panther to the Moroccan port of Agadir as a protest against French influence in Morocco and the Congo. On 21 July David Lloyd George, the British Chancellor of the Exchequer, warned in his Mansion House speech that Britain would not be treated as of no account where its interests were affected. Britannica writes that the crisis reconfirmed Anglo-French solidarity.

citations.quote: In 1911, Germany sent its gunboat Panther to the port of Agadir as a display of force and a protest against French influence in Morocco and the Congo.
Agadir Crisis: Lloyd George's Mansion House Speech 21 July, 1911
David Lloyd George, then British Chancellor of the Exchequer used the occasion of his speech at Mansion House to deliver a stern warning against further German expansion.

by allowing Britain to be treated where her interests were vitally affected as if she were of no account in the Cabinet of nations, then I say emphatically that peace at that price would be a humiliation
Franco-British solidarity was confirmed at the Algeciras Conference (1906) and reconfirmed in the Second Moroccan Crisis (1911).

events.title: Franz Ferdinand's plans to reorganise the monarchy
events.summary: The heir to the Habsburg throne considered reforms that would have strengthened the crown and weakened the Magyars' position over Hungary's other nationalities.
events.description: Archduke Franz Ferdinand, heir to the Austro-Hungarian throne, considered political reforms that would have strengthened the crown and weakened the position of the Magyars against the other nationalities in Hungary. Britannica writes that he believed any nationalist policy pursued by one part of the population endangered the multinational empire. Foster writes that his proposals for greater autonomy for the monarchy's South Slav territories challenged Serbian nationalist ambitions.

citations.quote: At home he thought of political reforms that would have strengthened the position of the crown and weakened that of the Magyars against the other nationalities in Hungary.
His plans were based on the realization that any nationalistic policy pursued by one section of the population would endanger the multinational Habsburg empire.
Franz Ferdinand’s proposals for greater political autonomy within the Monarchy’s South Slav territories posed a direct challenge to Serbian nationalist ambitions.

perspectives.wanted: He wanted to strengthen the crown, reduce Magyar dominance in Hungary and give the monarchy's South Slav territories more political autonomy.
perspectives.feared: He believed that a nationalist policy pursued by any one section of the population would endanger the multinational empire.

citations.quote: At home he thought of political reforms that would have strengthened the position of the crown and weakened that of the Magyars against the other nationalities in Hungary.
His plans were based on the realization that any nationalistic policy pursued by one section of the population would endanger the multinational Habsburg empire.
Franz Ferdinand’s proposals for greater political autonomy within the Monarchy’s South Slav territories posed a direct challenge to Serbian nationalist ambitions.

perspectives.wanted: Serbian nationalists regarded the Serbs of Bosnia-Herzegovina as part of a historic Greater Serbia.

citations.quote: Serbian nationalists proved the most antagonistic, perceiving Bosnia-Herzegovina’s large Serb minority as an integral part of a historic “Greater Serbia”.

events.title: Balkan Wars
events.summary: The Balkan Wars reduced Ottoman territory in Europe, enlarged Serbia and increased tensions between Serbia and Austria-Hungary.
events.description: The two Balkan Wars of 1912–1913 left the Ottoman Empire with only part of Thrace and Adrianople among its European territories. Serbia emerged larger, and tensions between Serbia and Austria-Hungary increased. In October 1913, Austria-Hungary issued an ultimatum demanding Serbia's withdrawal from the Albanian borderlands.

citations.quote: Balkan Wars, (1912–13), two successive military conflicts that deprived the Ottoman Empire of all its remaining territory in Europe except part of Thrace and the city of Adrianople (Edirne).
Following the Balkan Wars of 1912-1913, Serbia emerged as a larger and more assertive presence in south-east Europe.

The most alarming aspect of the war was the growth of tension between Austria-Hungary and Serbia. Serbia had extensive claims upon Albanian territory. Having obtained an assurance of German support, Austria-Hungary delivered an ultimatum on October 17, 1913, to compel Serbia to withdraw from the Albanian borderlands.

perspectives.wanted: Serbia's government turned toward Macedonia, where it considered an attack on Ottoman territory possible with Bulgarian support.
perspectives.feared: Serbia's government believed it could not challenge Austria-Hungary, despite resenting the exclusion of a future union with Bosnia and Herzegovina.

events.title: Franz Ferdinand and Sophie are assassinated in Sarajevo
events.summary: Gavrilo Princip killed Franz Ferdinand and Sophie in Sarajevo on 28 June 1914; anti-Serb protests and riots followed across Austria-Hungary.
events.description: On 28 June 1914, Gavrilo Princip assassinated Archduke Franz Ferdinand, heir to the Austro-Hungarian throne, and his wife Sophie in Sarajevo. Britannica writes that Serbian Prime Minister Nikola Pašić, an enemy of the Black Hand's leader Apis, had heard of the plot and warned the Austrian government, but that his message was too cautiously worded to be understood. Anti-Serb protests and riots followed throughout Austria-Hungary.

citations.quote: Gavrilo Princip (born July 25 [July 13, Old Style], 1894, Obljaj, Bosnia—died April 28, 1918, Theresienstadt, Austria) was a South Slav nationalist who assassinated Archduke Franz Ferdinand, heir to the Austro-Hungarian throne, and his consort, Sophie, Duchess von Hohenberg (née Chotek), at Sarajevo, Bosnia, on June 28, 1914.
Anti-Serb protests and riots followed throughout Austria-Hungary in the wake of the assassination.
Nikola Pašić, the Serbian prime minister and an enemy of Apis, heard of the plot and warned the Austrian government of it, but his message was too cautiously worded to be understood.

perspectives.wanted: Princip wanted to end Austro-Hungarian rule in the Balkans and unite the South Slavs in a federal nation, and believed that the first step must be killing a member of the Habsburg imperial family or a senior government official.
perspectives.remembered: In Yugoslavia, Princip came to be regarded as a "national hero."

citations.quote: Wanting to destroy Austro-Hungarian rule in the Balkans and to unite the South Slav peoples into a federal nation, he believed that the first step must be the assassination of a member of the Habsburg imperial family or a high official of the government.
In Yugoslavia—the South Slav state that he had envisioned—Princip came to be regarded as a national hero.

perspectives.wanted: Conrad von Hötzendorf and Foreign Minister Berchtold saw the assassination as an opportunity to humiliate Serbia and strengthen Austria-Hungary's prestige in the Balkans.
perspectives.feared: Emperor Franz Joseph believed Russian and Serbian Pan-Slavist agitation sought to weaken the Triple Alliance and destroy his empire.

citations.quote: The chief of the Austro-Hungarian general staff, Franz, Graf (count) Conrad von Hötzendorf, and the foreign minister, Leopold, Graf von Berchtold, saw the crime as the occasion for measures to humiliate Serbia and so to enhance Austria-Hungary’s prestige in the Balkans.

The attack directed against my poor nephew is the direct consequence of the agitation carried on by the Russian and Serbian Pan-Slavists whose sole aim is the weakening of the Triple Alliance and the destruction of my Empire.

The Royal Government cannot be made responsible for expressions of a private character, as for instance newspaper articles and the peaceable work of societies
The Royal Government was therefore painfully surprised by the assertions that citizens of Serbia had participated in the preparations of the outrage in Sarajevo.

events.title: Germany promises support to Austria-Hungary
events.summary: On 5–6 July, Germany assured Austria-Hungary of support for action against Serbia in what became known as the blank cheque.
events.description: On 5 July, Germany promised Austria-Hungary full support for a severe response to Serbia. On 6 July, Wilhelm II and Chancellor Bethmann-Hollweg reaffirmed that Germany would support whatever action Austria-Hungary considered necessary against Serbia, an assurance described as a blank cheque.

citations.quote: On 5 July, Germany promised Austria full support for a severe response against Serbia.

On July 6th, Wilhelm II and his Imperial Chancellor, Theobald von Bethmann-Hollweg, telegrammed Berchtold that Austria-Hungary could rely that Germany would support whatever action was necessary to deal with Serbia -- in effect offering von Berchtold a 'blank check.'

events.title: Austria-Hungary issues an ultimatum to Serbia
events.summary: Austria-Hungary demanded Serbian concessions, rejected Serbia’s reply and declared war.
events.description: Austria-Hungary issued an ultimatum to Serbia on 23 July with German backing. Serbia accepted most terms but rejected Austro-Hungarian participation in the assassination inquiry. Austria-Hungary rejected the reply and declared war on 28 July.

citations.quote: With the guarantee of German backing, Austria-Hungary issued an ultimatum on 23 July, intent on starting a war with Serbia.

events.title: Russia orders general mobilization
events.summary: Russia ordered general mobilization on 30 July, and Germany demanded that it halt its preparations.
events.description: Russia ordered general mobilization on 30 July as Austria-Hungary ordered mobilization on its Russian frontier. Germany issued an ultimatum on 31 July demanding that Russia halt its mobilization.

citations.quote: Russia then ordered partial mobilization against Austria-Hungary, and on July 30, when Austria-Hungary was riposting conventionally with an order of mobilization on its Russian frontier, Russia ordered general mobilization.

events.title: Germany declares war on Russia

events.title: Germany invades Belgium
events.summary: Germany invaded Belgium on 4 August after Belgium refused passage to German troops.

chains.title: The road to World War I, 1878–1914
chains.description: This chain traces disputes over Bosnia and Serbian nationalism through the Sarajevo assassination to mobilization and British entry into the war. Its links distinguish documented decisions from disputed interpretations of responsibility.

chains.title: The July Crisis: from Sarajevo to a European war
chains.description: The Sarajevo assassination was followed by German support for Austria-Hungary, an ultimatum to Serbia, Russian mobilization and German declarations of war. Germany's invasion of Belgium contributed to Britain's decision to enter the war.

chains.title: How Europe's alliances formed, 1879–1914
chains.description: This chain connects alliance treaties, German planning for war against France and Russia, and the advance through Belgium in 1914.
